IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01022
Without recognising this other kind of time—different from the chronological time we measure through planetary movements—we can hardly understand the Shiite view of prophecy.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01023

Consider how sacred history is divided into cycles. In Twelver Shiism, each great prophet is followed by twelve Imams, most of whose names can be linked to names in the Bible. In Ismailism, each prophet has seven Imams, and the Great Resurrection proclaimed at Alamut in 1164 is understood as taking place in the middle of our Aeon, our great age of the world. Anyone who fails to recognise that these cycles belong to the time of sacred history will dismiss them as inventions of the mind. A history or archaeology textbook may then appear to “disprove” them.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01024
But that objection misses the point: the same names are being used, on the two sides, to speak about different kinds of events.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01025

The events of sacred history remain open to the future because, according to a well-known saying attributed to the Prophet, the Qur’an has seven inner depths of meaning (see Chapter V and Book IV, Chapter II, below). This belief is foundational to Shiism. It gives Shiite spiritual life a direction similar to that which the idea of the Paraclete gives certain forms of Christianity. After the Prophet, the Hidden Imam assumed both the name and the role of the Paraclete. Shiite consciousness therefore remains open to expectation and to intimations of what is still to come.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01026

By contrast, the majority tradition in Islam lives by the established certainties of the Law, regarded as complete and definitively expressed. The Imam will not bring a new sharia, a new religious law; that would contradict the whole point.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01027

Instead, he will “open” the spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis) of the revelation given to Muhammad and of all earlier revelations. This is ta'wil: the uncovering of their inner meaning. Meanwhile, for ten centuries already, as measured by our ordinary time, the Imamate has been in concealment, or ghaybat. The Imams can be seen only in dreams or in the visionary insight of a deeply personal prayer (munajat).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01028
Yet even in such encounters they can reveal the meaning of a passage or a prayer. That is enough to give the person who receives their confidence a certainty no worldly power can shake.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01029
We will encounter more than one example in this book.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01030

We can certainly speak of the authority of the Imam and the Imams. But this is an entirely spiritual authority, not another kind of power competing with the powers of this world. Its foundation is the prophetic teaching that every outward appearance (zahir) has a hidden, inner meaning (batin). That claim alone is enough to alarm the majority tradition of Islam, much as the teachings of Montanus or Joachim of Fiore once alarmed the Christian world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01031

Yet in Islam, the claim reaches back to a time before the Prophet himself expressed it: to his initiation into his own calling as a prophet. This brings us back to Salman Parsi—Salman the Persian, also called Salman Pak, Salman the Pure. We have met this mysterious figure before. He stands at the very heart of the spiritual landscape of Iranian Islam.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01032

We can now better understand the story of Salman, the son of a Zoroastrian knight from Fars. He sets out in search of the True Prophet, finds him in Arabia, and helps awaken him to his prophetic calling. He does so by helping him become aware of the spiritual states experienced by earlier prophets and bring those states to life within himself.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01033

In the Shiite esoteric understanding of Islam, Salman's role as a companion in spiritual initiation is an angelic ministry. It means that ta'wil—the return from the outward words to their hidden meaning, a meaning that speaks to the person discovering it here and now—belongs to Islam from its very beginnings.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01034

Through Salman's visible, earthly presence, this angelic ministry gives form to the bond that a manifestation of God establishes between the Prophet and the “Supreme Namus” (Nomos). This is the Angel of Revelation who, acting as the Paraclete, invests the Prophet with his mission. That bond is the source, in Islam, of what we have called the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01035

If the mystic's calling is to relive the Prophet's spiritual state, and if this prophetic dimension of mystical life rests on revelation's hidden meaning, then the mystic also needs a Salman beside him. Or, more precisely, he must find his way back to the “Salman within himself”—the “Salman of the small world within,” as a very early Ismaili treatise puts it. That is how he establishes his inner relationship with the Imam, who is both the source and the guarantee of the hidden meaning. This is why the Imam is more than any one of his earthly appearances.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01036

Each Imam who was visible for a time, each figure in the complete circle of Twelve, was the earthly point of contact with an eternal Imam, and the doorway leading to him. In himself, the Imam is the eternal manifestation of God (tajalli, mazhar), the heavenly Human Being (Anthropos), the figure through which God is shown in human form. Some Ismaili Shiite writings call him Melchizedek—a name that tells us a great deal about the image these writers have in mind and where it comes from.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01037

Because the Imam exists in this heavenly way, he can also be described as the spiritual person's invisible inner guide (see Chapter VII below). We need to keep all of this in mind when Haydar Amoli speaks of Sufism as true Shiism, as we noted earlier (see also Book IV, Chapter I). That identification has left its mark on the whole spiritual history of Iran.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01038

Prophetic inspiration, then, has not come to an end: it remains possible under another name. The highest point of mystical experience is entry into the “contemplative prophethood” belonging to the cycle of walayat—the continuing life of spiritual guidance and closeness to God. The mystic reaches this point by taking the meaning of revelation deeply into himself, guided by the Imam, who both embodies and reveals that meaning. The idea of the Imam thus allows Shiite thought to hold two convictions together. Muhammad is the “Seal of Prophecy,” the last prophet to bring a revealed law; yet something new can still happen.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01039

Indeed, the new event is something the spiritual person becomes. So when we ask, “Must sacred history be confined to past events, or can it become an inner experience?”, the Shiite answer is that sacred history continues precisely through this inward transformation. That is how the cycle of walayat is fulfilled.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01040

This also explains why we have spent so much time examining the Holy Book and the ways its meaning is uncovered. Far from being a detour, that discussion leads directly to the position I want to bring together in the following pages.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01041

There is an ambiguity in what we mean by history and historical research. We usually agree that a historian discussing a philosopher's teaching should tell us what that philosopher actually said. To criticize those ideas or declare them mistaken is to speak as a philosopher, not simply as a historian.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01042

Yet we sometimes hear scholars, speaking in the name of history, deny that a particular Imam could have said something attributed to him. They may argue, for instance, that the words used in a saying belong to a vocabulary introduced only later, when Greek philosophical works were translated into Syriac and Arabic.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01043

Even if that argument were decisive, one fact would remain: for more than thirteen centuries, Shiite believers have heard the voices of their Imams in these sayings. To insist that an Imam never spoke those words is to challenge what Shiite consciousness has experienced. It is to deny its right to hear the words in that way and, with it, the truth of that experience.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01044

Whatever force such a historical argument may have today, it cannot undo the fact that for more than thirteen centuries Shiite consciousness has heard its Imams speaking through these words. That hearing is itself part of its history—its own inner history, the cycle of walayat. The sayings are heard as the Imams' words because, given what they say and what the Imams are understood to be, Shiite believers can hear them only as the words of the Imams. The modern challenge threatens to silence that voice, interrupt that history, and bring it to an end.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01045

Would that be the strange achievement of a historical science that could accept a historical reality (res historica) only after turning it into a dead thing (res mortua)? Such a science might not realize that it too is continuing the history of its subject—but in the manner of someone following a funeral procession that the science itself has arranged. The believer, by contrast, continues that history by living it: the tradition is part of the believer's life, just as the believer is part of its continuing life.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01046

This is why I have turned to the method known as phenomenology: the attempt to understand an experience as it appears to the people who live it. To use the well-known Greek expression sozein ta phainomena, the task is to “save the phenomena.” That means doing justice to what appears by uncovering the hidden intentions that give it meaning and allow it to appear in the first place. The Arabic expression kashf al-mahjub, “unveiling what was hidden,” points to something similar. It is the title of many Arabic and Persian works on philosophy and mystical experience.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01047

Working in this way, the scholar can describe the history that takes shape within the believer's own experience. Rather than telling that experience in advance what it must mean, the scholar lets it appear as it appears to the believer. Historical criticism begins by placing a religious reality into ordinary history; in doing so, it gives that reality a history and a form of time that may never have belonged to it.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01048

The study of lived experience lets the religious reality tell its own story, in the kind of time proper to it. The living reality of the Imam must therefore be sought in the testimony of those who experience or have experienced him. For them, the Imam is their history; through their lives, they also reveal what that history means.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01049

Questioning their testimony may produce what we call scientific results. But if we make the religious experience fit a time and a history alien to it, we change its character and meaning at the very moment we claim to explain it.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01050

We must be able to preserve its original meaning without giving up scholarly care. I have called this phenomenology, but I remember an eminent Iranian Shiite shaykh who had never heard that word and nevertheless went straight to the heart of the matter. He was speaking about scholars who questioned the authenticity of parts of the Nahj al-balagha, the collection of sermons, conversations, and letters attributed to the First Imam. He said: “Yes, I know the criticisms made of this book.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01051
“But I also know this: whoever held the pen that wrote the text we read today, at that moment it was the Imam who was speaking.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01052
If a scholar wishes to hear the Imam speak, rather than silence him by forcing him into a history that is not his own, the scholar too must listen at that moment.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01053

But “that moment” cannot be fixed by a date in the continuous timeline of ordinary history. It is the moment when an experience comes alive in consciousness, within the particular kind of time that belongs to that consciousness.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01054

Why, then, is what Shiite consciousness experiences not simply a historical fact that falls somewhere on the timeline? Why does it create its own history—even to the point that proving a saying to be of later date would not change this history at all? Because the Imams, as members of the complete spiritual reality of Muhammad (Haqiqat muhammadiya), belong through both their persons and their teachings to spiritual worlds.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01055

The events connected with them are events of a kind found in those worlds alone. As we have already seen, theirs is not an outward history like that of Julius Caesar. Neither the Imam's true person nor the content of his teaching appears on the ordinary “stage of historical events” as Caesar and his deeds do.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01056

The Imam himself, even when invisible to the senses, is the stage on which the events unfold: the place of manifestation (mazhar). He can be that place only in the consciousness of people to whom he appears as Imam. If we look for him somewhere else, and presume to tell believers what they ought to have believed or seen if only they had occupied our position as critical scholars, we destroy the very experience we set out to understand. Inevitably, we come away empty-handed.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01057

Some of the many Shiite traditions (hadith) can be understood in this light. The Imam is the form through which all spiritual wisdom and knowledge of sacred realities are perceived. A saying or vision experienced under his inspiration “at that moment” would therefore naturally come to be written down in his name. That expresses a profound inner truth. It belongs to the same world of meaning as the hadith qudsi, a sacred or divinely inspired report. This is what makes the Imam's person the history of Shiite consciousness and makes that consciousness the interpreter of the meaning of the Imam. It also agrees with the way the Fifth Imam describes the relation between revelation and its readers.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01058
To understand and explain this, a study of Shiite experience comes close to the concerns of the school called Formgeschichte, the study of how traditional accounts take shape and are passed down.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01059

First, however, we must distinguish what is historically true in the ordinary sense from what remains true as a lived spiritual experience. The latter concerns events that, although fully real to those who experience them, do not belong to the familiar dimension of historical time.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01060

Only by being so careful about our method can we understand the many texts concerning the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, without dismissing them as myth or legend, or demanding that they be ordinary historical records. We can then preserve the kind of reality that belongs to events in the world where the Twelfth Imam lives.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01061

Consider another example, one of great importance to the spiritual self-understanding of Iran: Suhrawardi. He set out to restore the wisdom of the sages of ancient Persia and claimed them as his spiritual ancestors. Modern historical criticism is free to regard that ancestry as an idea he imagined.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01062

Yet Suhrawardi genuinely knew some elements of pre-Islamic Persian wisdom. More importantly, no amount of criticism can change what happened to the meaning of ancient Iran after him. For the thinkers of Islamic Persia, ancient Iran came to mean something new. Even if he could not establish a line of descent that would satisfy modern historical methods, Suhrawardi demonstrated his spiritual ancestry by bringing something back to life. In his followers, that recovered inheritance became essential to Iran's philosophical and spiritual identity (see Book II below).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01063

These followers are known as the Illuminationists (Ishraqiyun), the sages of light. Their philosophy of illumination, or “Eastern wisdom” (ishraq), came together with the Shiite understanding of the Imams in Iran well before the School of Isfahan in the sixteenth century. That meeting is a spiritual event of special importance.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01064

As we shall see, the Neoplatonic sages of Persia perceive the continuation of sacred history in the very act of knowing. In their understanding, knowing depends on the Angel of Revelation, Gabriel, being the same as the Angel of Knowledge. The “Active Intelligence,” which makes understanding possible, and the Holy Spirit are understood as one and the same spiritual being. This did not, as some have too quickly claimed, reduce the Spirit to reason by repeating a development familiar in the West.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01065

Quite the opposite happened. These thinkers did not construct a “philosophy of history” that tries to explain the great movements of history by weaving abstract arguments around them. They developed what we might call a wisdom of the Holy Spirit. It remained open to renewed prophetic insight, as each individual discovered the deeper meaning of revelation in a living experience.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01066

Precisely because of these shared concerns, this wisdom of the Holy Spirit could enter into a dialogue, with consequences we cannot foresee, with Western traditions of divine wisdom that have also been guided by the idea of the Paraclete. It is inseparable from a whole understanding of the human mind and its powers: the angelic soul, the prophetic soul, the soul associated with Gabriel. This understanding of the human person fits a teaching about prophecy that calls for an account of what it means to be human as a prophetic being.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
en-book-1-ch-4-s5
5. Spiritual Understanding and the Different Forms of Time in Semnani and Qazi Sa'id Qummi
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01067

All these ideas require us to rethink what time is. They include the identity of the Angel of Knowledge with the Angel of Revelation, and of the Active Intelligence with the Holy Spirit—an identity at the heart of spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis). They include the possibility that prophetic inspiration remains open, through what Semnani will call “the Muhammad within you.” They include the hidden demands of revelation's inner meaning, whose prophetic truth is higher and more real than any attempt to confine an accomplished event to history. And they include the recognition that outward events can symbolize events of the soul, their meanings echoing through one “level of the universe” after another (see Section 2 above).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01068

Taken together, these ideas require us to change our understanding of a single, uniform flow of time. We have already suggested that modern philosophy, despite trying to separate human historical time from the time of nature, may actually have made human beings even more subject to nature's way of thinking.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01069

To see ordinary historical time as a fall of time into history, we first need to recognize another kind of time. It must be different from the time in which we date the events of our world. It must be qualitative time: the inner time of psychological and spiritual life, not the quantitative time of a continuous sequence measured in equal units by clocks and calendars.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01070
It is remarkable that one of the greatest spiritual teachers of fourteenth-century Iran, Ala al-Dawla Semnani, already understood this distinction and had precise terms for it.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01071

We will examine some of his most important writings later (Book IV, Chapter IV). He reached this understanding by interpreting the hidden meaning of the Qur'an. His starting point was the verse: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within their own souls” (41:53).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01072

On the horizons (afaq) means in the cosmos: the outer world of objects, of events and of history. Within their souls (anfos) means in the inner world, the world of spiritual and psychological experience. Accordingly, Semnani distinguishes two forms of time. There is zaman afaqi, the time of the horizons: chronological time, the time of outward history and its events. And there is zaman anfosi, the time within the soul: the time of inner events, symbolic histories and personal existence.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01073

The two are related through correspondences—what we may call the “symbolism of the worlds.” This makes it possible to discover the spiritual meaning of things and events “in Heaven.” Such understanding requires us to reach a different level of awareness, both in our understanding of the universe and in our own inner life. It is not the same as allegory, which merely replaces one outward image with another while remaining at the same level of meaning. As we shall see, Semnani's remarkable interpretation of the prophets as living realities within the soul moves through the different depths of this newly opened inner world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01074

He never tires of insisting that the events understood inwardly are still real events, taking place in real time. That time, however, is not the time of the horizons, zaman afaqi: the continuous, measurable time of the cosmos, marked by the movement of the stars. It is zaman anfosi, the inner time of spiritual experience. It is the time of events in the soul, measured neither by uniform units nor by the revolutions of heavenly bodies.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01075

To suggest just how different these two forms of time are, Semnani cites a Qur'anic verse that echoes one of our Psalms: “A day with your Lord is like a thousand years of the time you count” (22:46). Moving from the time of the world's history to the time of the soul means crossing a boundary between two measures of reality that cannot simply be compared.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01076

This turning of time marks the passage into a new level of awareness. It requires a change in the person from within, which is why it cannot be reduced to interpreting stories as allegories. The turning of time both makes possible and results from bringing the meaning of outward historical events into the inner life. Those events are now experienced in the time of the soul, the “time of your Lord.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01077

This change of time also allows our sages to answer an objection to the Shiite teaching that the Qur'an, as God's eternal Word, has an eternal inner meaning. The objection is that, if the Qur'an is eternal, the events it recounts must somehow have happened before the people involved were born (see Book IV, Chapter II).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01078

But this objection assumes there is only one kind of time: physical time, continuous, measurable and irreversible, the outward time of world history (zaman afaqi). It overlooks the relationship between a symbolic account (hikayat) and the reality it reflects. Unable to recognize how different worlds correspond to one another, the objector pushes time further into its “fall into history.” For it is historical time, with its sequence of earlier and later events, that makes the past recede behind us.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01079
Another kind of time is possible: a time in which what comes before and what comes after can be present together.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01080

We have again spoken of the “symbolism of the worlds.” To turn from one kind of time to another requires a transformation of the person. At the same time, that transformation frees inner powers of perception that had been inactive, allowing the spiritual self to enter other worlds—worlds beyond the senses, where time itself is different. “Here, my son,” Parsifal is told, “time becomes space.” This other time becomes an other space.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01081

Anyone, or any culture, unable or unwilling to enter such a world will likewise be unable to accept spiritual events as real in their own right. These events belong to the different “levels of the universe” discussed earlier. That is precisely what the symbolism of the worlds means. It can be recognized only through spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis). The discovery of the Holy Book's inner meaning therefore goes hand in hand with the perception of other forms of time. Once those forms are recognized, we are no longer forced to choose between saying that an account is either myth or ordinary history.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01082

We have just seen how closely Semnani, a master of the spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an, examined this problem. We could follow its many forms throughout the history of Iranian Islamic wisdom. Among the thinkers in that tradition, however, the question of different kinds of time seems to have occupied Qazi Sa'id Qummi more deeply than most. We have already met him as one of the outstanding Shiite thinkers of Safavid Persia.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01083

In his extensive, still unpublished commentary on Ibn Babuyeh's Kitab al-Tawhid (Book of God's Oneness), one of the oldest and most important works of Shiite thought, Qazi Sa'id offered his own account of the problem. He used somewhat different concepts from Semnani.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01084

He knew very well that he was challenging an old assumption in a certain kind of metaphysics: the belief that every spiritual world must, by its very nature, be motionless and unchanging. Qazi Sa'id followed a long tradition of Islamic spiritual philosophy that understood existence differently. For him, the deepest question was not simply the meaning of the verb to be (esse, wujud) or the noun a being (ens, mawjud). It was the divine command “Be!” (KN, Esto!), the imperative that brings beings into existence.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01085

Because this command is constantly renewed, it continually draws every existing thing—every being and its very act of existing—away from the pull of nothingness. Nothing in the created universe is sufficient unto itself. No created being contains within itself the power to keep itself in existence. This is as true of spiritual worlds as it is of the material world. All are carried by a vast upward movement of the creative command, lifting them away from the weight of their own tendency towards non-being.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01086
We can make sense of this only if we accept that movement also belongs to the higher spiritual worlds: a movement of the spirit or of meaning (harakat ruhaniya, ma'nawiya).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01087
“But,” our author says, “this is extremely difficult to understand, which is why you see most philosophers who rely on abstract reasoning reject the idea.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01088
Because this movement belongs to existence itself, Qazi Sa'id argues that we must recognize three kinds of time.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01089

Dense time, or “opaque time” (zaman kathif), is the time of material beings. It is the duration of physical movements carried out by physical things and observed through the senses. It is the kind of time we can measure, in one way or another, by the movements of heavenly bodies. It corresponds to Semnani's zaman afaqi, the time of the horizons.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01091

Subtle time (zaman latif) is the duration of movements made by spiritual beings. For these thinkers, even physical motion, including the movement of the stars, ultimately has its source in a spiritual movement. More generally, subtle time belongs to everything that moves or changes within the world of the Soul. That includes both the higher Malakut, the world of the heavenly angels (Angeli caelestes), understood as the souls that move the heavens, and the lower Malakut, the world of human souls.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01092

These movements include revelations, inspirations and visions received by prophets and other spiritual people, and the wonders and miracles they perform. In short, they include all the events of sacred history. Such events do not take place in the physical world and therefore do not belong to its time. They take place in the time and space of the Malakut, the world of the Soul as a whole.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01093

This is the alam al-mithal, which we have already explained is best called the imaginal world (mundus imaginalis). Qazi Sa'id, like other thinkers in this tradition, is careful to insist that the “world of Image and Imagination” (alam al-khayal wa'l-mithal) is not imaginary in the sense of being unreal. It has its own genuine existence (mawjud) and its own way of being perceived: through the imaginative power that is able to encounter its images.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01094

Unless our understanding of reality makes room for this intermediate world of the Soul, we cannot grasp what is real in visions of divine manifestations, understand symbolic stories, or recognize the world of “subtle bodies.” Without that world, we cannot understand the spiritual meaning of the revelations concerning the “Lesser Resurrection” (Qiyamat sughra) and the “Greater Resurrection” (Qiyamat kubra). None of these things “enters the history” of our world, yet they are not mere myths. This is why their time cannot be identical to ours. When we try to express the qualitative time of the Malakut in the units of dense, physical time, it appears to exceed every normal measure. Qazi Sa'id sees a hint of this change from chronological to subtle time in the Qur'anic verse that speaks of “a day whose length is a thousand years by your reckoning” (32:4). This subtle time is the same form of time Semnani called zaman anfosi, the inner time of the soul, and associated with a corresponding Qur'anic verse (22:46).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01095

Still subtler time, or “absolutely subtle time” (zaman altaf), belongs to the highest spiritual realities: the pure angelic Intelligences (Angeli intellectuales), the most sacred Lights, the world of the Jabarut. This is the time referred to in the Qur'anic verse about “the degrees by which the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose length is fifty thousand years” (70:4). In Ismaili spiritual philosophy, fifty thousand years also symbolizes the full duration of a cycle. This is the Aevum mundi, the Aion: the great age or world-time.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01096
These three kinds of time can be compared with distinctions made by other Islamic thinkers and inherited from the Neoplatonists. Qazi Sa'id draws two conclusions from them.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01097

First, the Creator, the source who brings existence into being, is himself beyond existence as created beings know it—utterly transcendent (monazzah, hyperousion). He therefore cannot be measured against anything in the three worlds, or against any of their three forms of time.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01098

Second, the very possibility of moving from one kind of time to another depends on the way these worlds correspond to one another. Every thing in the physical world (molk) has its own Malakut, the spiritual reality that governs it. And each of those spiritual realities in turn has its Jabarut. In other words, every thing we perceive through the senses has an Image (mithal) in the imaginal world of the Malakut. Every such Image, in turn, has an original reality made of pure light.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01099

That original reality is the divine Word (Kalimat ilahiya), the divine command addressed to each created being. It sustains that being in existence and leads it towards its fulfilment. It stands as its witness before God and humanity. It is at once the being's innermost, hidden reality (batin) and the reality placed before it, the one that “goes ahead” (moqaddam) and guides its existence.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01100

We will see in Chapter VII that this is precisely how the Imam stands at the centre of the most deeply personal forms of Shiite spirituality: as the heavenly pole of each being, the point around which that being's own spiritual history turns.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01101

Later, we will examine one account, among others, of a living experience of this passage from the dense time of the visible world to the subtle time of the imaginal world. It is the “Tradition of the White Cloud,” which Qazi Sa'id Qummi comments on with great insight. A few companions are carried by the Imam on a mysterious journey into the Malakut. Suddenly, events that belong to different dates in ordinary history become present together for them. They find themselves eyewitnesses to things that chronological history recounts as past or announces as future (see Book V, Chapter III).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01102
To sum up Qazi Sa'id's account, the three kinds of time belong to three worlds, each of which has many levels of its own.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01103

First comes the world of the senses (alam hissi), the molk. Second comes the world of the Soul, the Malakut, the imaginal world. Third comes the world of Intelligence, the Nous or Jabarut, where there are pure realities of thought and pure Lights.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01104

The forms of the world of the senses come from the Soul; the Soul comes from Intelligence; and Intelligence comes from God. That first outpouring from God is the primordial Reality of Muhammad (Haqiqat muhammadiya). The Prophet describes it in different ways. Sometimes he says, “The first thing God created was Intelligence”; at other times, “My light.” The names used for these three worlds vary among our sages, but the underlying pattern remains the same. Suhrawardi himself had already stressed how constant it is.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01105

Something from each of these three worlds is present in the human being. As a person develops spiritually, this makes it possible at least to glimpse the change from one kind of time into another. These other times become other spaces: places where events unfold that, judged only by ordinary historical time and the laws of our physical world, could seem unreal. For the spiritual traveller, however, an outward story can be understood as a real symbolic history—a hikayat, a story that reflects the real things of other worlds. This is what I mean by intelligentia spiritualis: spiritual understanding.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01106

The idea of the time of the soul—whether we call it zaman anfosi, as Semnani does, or zaman latif, “subtle time,” as Qazi Sa'id does—helps us avoid confusing fundamentally different kinds of time. It is the time of manifestations of God and of the soul's deepest, original events. Those events arrive in sudden, recurring moments, not in a continuous chain.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01107

We cannot use them to build an uninterrupted historical narrative or a conventional philosophy of history, in which one cause leads to another and the entire sequence gives us a satisfying, perhaps reassuring, rational explanation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01108

Consider the difference between these spiritual events and the Incarnation, which Christian chronology places at a particular point in time, the beginning of our era. Manifestations of God and visionary events do not enter outward history in the same way. They cannot be fitted into its measurements. World history can reach the witnesses of these experiences, but not the spiritual events themselves. It is therefore always free to reject the witnesses' accounts of worlds that lie beyond its own reach.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01109
Yet the true place and content of such an event are not “nothing but” the witness's soul. They are nothing less than that soul.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01110

We must therefore decide, once and for all, where—and in what kind of time—we should seek those who are truly alive, those who genuinely live in the present. Once we have made that decision, we can understand how a manifestation of God, although beyond ordinary history, can give shape to a cycle or a sequence of cycles within sacred history. Sacred history, at its heart, is symbolic history.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01111

This way of understanding history differs fundamentally from what we ordinarily call a “philosophy of history.” It is not built by turning observed events into concepts or general “laws of history.” Nor does it arise simply from gathering evidence about the physical world. We have already discussed how the numbers seven and twelve shape the understandings of the Imams in Ismailism and Twelver Shiism respectively. These numbers express a cosmic order because they correspond to the rhythm of experience as it is lived.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01112

The image shaped by these numbers is not something the soul learns from outward events. It is the very means by which the soul perceives events at all: an image already present within it, enabling it to give form to what it encounters and to make sense of what it observes. The image does not come from the facts; rather, it gives the facts the form through which they can be understood. For these sages, this expresses the priority of the Malakut over the molk: the spiritual reality comes first, at the level of being itself.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01113

A modern thinker might describe the imaginal as a basic form that the mind brings to experience, something already present before any particular observation, without which there could be no imago mundi, no image of the world. Whatever name we give it, this prior form is often overlooked by supposedly “objective” historical science, which tries to draw a philosophy from “the facts,” even though that philosophy is always open to challenge.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01114
By contrast, an imago mundi gives the facts symbolic form. We may understand a symbol or fail to understand it, but we cannot simply “disprove” a symbol.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01115

The cycles of sacred history considered in Shiite teachings on prophecy, together with the astronomical cycles that correspond to them, belong to such an image of the world. Ismaili cyclical time, for example, does not move in the same direction as our historical time, towards old age, death and disappearance. It leads the being back towards its origin; it makes up for an eternity that the being has not yet fully reached. This is not a theory drawn from measurable historical facts. It is a way of perceiving the “facts” of the Malakut.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01116
The same point applies, incidentally, to all the traditional sciences that depend on a culture's imago mundi, its picture of how the world is ordered.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01117

Consider astrology. We miss what astrology originally meant if, instead of recovering the image of the world through which this intuitive knowledge arranged the stars and understood their roles, we treat it as an ordinary rational science. We then try to judge the supposed influence of the stars through familiar chains of physical cause and effect, although that is not the kind of influence this system was designed to express. Astrology may have taken on that form in its later decline, but that is a different matter.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01118

I mention it only as an example. To understand an imago mundi and the way it interprets the world—its interpretatio mundi—we must first distinguish that picture and its way of interpretation from the particular material they interpret. We have to understand how they establish the very object of their attention. As Schiller wrote, “The stars of your destiny are in your heart.” In the heart of the person who possesses inner spiritual knowledge are the stars and cycles of prophetic history. Semnani's entire interpretation of hidden meaning will consist in discovering the figures of prophecy within the person.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01119

This is why the familiar oppositions now fall away. Prophetic religion and mystical religion are no longer opposites, because the visions and manifestations of God that begin a prophetic calling are themselves the highest experiences of mystical life. Nor do religion and philosophy, or belief and knowledge, have to stand apart. The Imam, whose walayat is the inner meaning of the prophetic message, is himself the Perfect Sage, the human being raised to an angelic form of life (Insan malaki, Homo angelicus). And the sage of divine wisdom (hakim ilahi) is, in turn, a prophetic philosopher.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01120

The idea that the philosopher and the mystic have a prophetic calling expresses a deep conviction: the Holy Spirit has not stopped inspiring human beings. That inspiration will continue for as long as the cycle of walayat endures. It will not bring a new revealed law. What it will bring into the open is meaning—the hidden meaning of all revelations.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01121

We have already heard the Fifth Imam declare that the Holy Book is alive for ever. His declaration rests on the belief that this deeper meaning comes to life again and again in every faithful person whose “heart has been tested.” The spiritual reality of the Holy Book is the same kind of reality that brought forth the Christian figures we discussed earlier.
